title: Do models share blind spots in their refusal direction? Homogeneity of the safety linear feature across model families

# Do models share blind spots in their refusal direction? Homogeneity of the safety linear feature across model families

**Problem:** The 'Artificial Hivemind' result (NeurIPS 2025 Best Paper) shows 70+ LLMs are homogeneous on open-ended outputs, but it is unknown whether their safety-critical internal features are also shared. If independently trained open models encode refusal along correlated activation directions, then an adversarial input or steering vector found on one model could transfer to many, creating a systemic, correlated jailbreak surface.

**Direction:** Take 4-6 small open-weight chat models (e.g. Llama-3-8B, Qwen2.5-7B, Mistral-7B, Gemma-2-9B, Phi). On a shared harmful/harmless prompt set, extract each model's refusal direction via difference-of-means on residual-stream activations (a cheap, well-documented technique). Then measure cross-model alignment: project one model's refusal direction into another's space (via a learned linear map fit on shared prompt activations) and test whether ablating the transferred direction degrades refusal. Quantify a 'safety homogeneity' score and compare to output-level homogeneity.

**Why it matters:** If safety features are homogeneous, a single open-source attack generalizes across the ecosystem (concentration risk). This is a medium-horizon systemic threat that frontier labs deprioritize because each lab only cares about its own model. No training, no proprietary data, runs on one GPU with hooks on small models — high counterfactual value.

**Relevant context:** Bridges model_homogeneity (Artificial Hivemind, Infinity-Chat, NeurIPS 2025 Best Paper, arxiv 2510.22954) with adversarial_robustness/mech_interp (refusal-direction extraction, difference-of-means; shallow alignment, Qi et al. title: Steering-vector sandbagging: can an activation direction make a model deliberately underperform, and does noise injection catch it?

# Steering-vector sandbagging: can an activation direction make a model deliberately underperform, and does noise injection catch it?

**Problem:** Sandbagging detection (Noise Injection, NeurIPS 2025) was demonstrated against prompt/fine-tuning-induced sandbagging. It is unknown whether sandbagging induced purely by an inference-time steering vector (a representation-engineering intervention) produces the same noise-injection signature, or whether steering creates a qualitatively different, harder-to-detect form of capability concealment.

**Direction:** Use contrastive activation addition to build an 'underperform/play-dumb' steering vector on a small open model (compute it from paired 'answer fully' vs 'answer poorly' completions). Apply it during a capability eval (e.g. MMLU subset, GSM8K subset) to induce graded sandbagging. Then run the published noise-injection detector (add Gaussian noise to weights at increasing magnitudes, watch for anomalous accuracy rebound) and ask: does steering-induced sandbagging show the same rebound curve as prompt-induced sandbagging? Compare detection ROC across induction methods.

**Why it matters:** If steering-induced sandbagging evades a state-of-the-art detector, it reveals a gap: control evals must account for representation-level concealment, not just behavioral or fine-tuning-based. This is a model-organism study scoped to a 30h slice using an existing open model — exactly the kind of work valuable outside a lab.

# CoT-monitor blind spot audit: do diverse open models converge on the SAME unfaithful rationalizations?

**Problem:** CoT monitoring is more informative than action-only monitoring, but if models are homogeneous (Artificial Hivemind), they may produce the same post-hoc rationalizations for the same biased decisions — meaning a CoT monitor trained on one model's failures would share its blind spots and a population of monitors offers no real diversity.

# Does shallow alignment leave a shallow probe? Layer-and-token map of where refusal lives vs where sandbagging hides

**Problem:** Shallow alignment (Qi et al.) shows refusal is concentrated in the first few output tokens. Separately, control needs activation probes that catch misbehavior in real time. Map probe accuracy as a heatmap over (layer, token position). Then test a prefilling attack (force a compliant prefix) and check whether the probe's accuracy collapses at exactly the positions where the shallow guardrail is bypassed.

**Why it matters:** If safety probes are only trustworthy in the shallow region, then activation-based jailbreak detection (a heavily promoted cheap defense) is structurally fragile against prefilling. This connects a known vulnerability to monitoring design — valuable infrastructure insight needing only one GPU and hooks.
